units.title: 4.1 Atomic structure and the periodic table

topics.title: 4.1.1 A simple model of the atom, symbols, relative atomic mass, electronic charge and isotopes

outcomes.text: State that atoms are the smallest part of an element and are shown by chemical symbols in the periodic table.
Explain that compounds form by chemical reactions, hold elements in fixed proportions, and can only be split by reactions.
Name elements and compounds and write word equations, formulae and balanced symbol equations (half and ionic equations at higher tier).
Distinguish a mixture from a compound and say the chemical properties of each part are unchanged.
Describe filtration, crystallisation, simple and fractional distillation and chromatography, and pick a method for a given mixture.
Describe the plum pudding model and why the alpha scattering experiment replaced it with the nuclear model.
Describe Bohr's orbiting electrons and the discovery of the proton and neutron.
Give the relative charges of protons, neutrons and electrons and state atoms are neutral.
Define atomic number as the number of protons and use it to tell elements apart.
Give the size of an atom and nucleus and say nearly all the mass is in the nucleus.
Define mass number and isotopes, and work out protons, neutrons and electrons in an atom or ion.
Relate the size and scale of atoms to objects in the physical world.
Explain relative atomic mass as an average that accounts for isotope abundance, and calculate it from percentages.
Fill energy levels from the lowest outwards and write electronic structures of the first twenty elements as numbers and diagrams.

topics.title: 4.1.2 The periodic table

outcomes.text: Explain that elements are ordered by atomic number and grouped by similar properties and outer electrons.
Predict reactions and reactivity from an element's position in the table.
Describe how early tables used atomic weights, and how Mendeleev left gaps and reordered elements.
Explain how discovered elements and isotope knowledge supported Mendeleev's predictions.
Say metals form positive ions, non-metals do not, and where each sits in the table.
Explain differences in properties and reactions of metals and non-metals using atomic structure.
Explain why noble gases are unreactive using their full outer shells.
State and use the trend of rising boiling points down Group 0.
Describe reactions of lithium, sodium and potassium with oxygen, chlorine and water.
Explain why reactivity rises down Group 1 and predict properties from the trend.
Describe halogens as non-metal diatomic molecules with seven outer electrons.
Describe compounds formed when chlorine, bromine and iodine react with metals and non-metals.
State trends down Group 7: higher melting and boiling points, lower reactivity.
Explain displacement of a less reactive halogen by a more reactive one.

topics.title: 4.1.3 Properties of transition metals (chemistry only)

outcomes.text: Compare transition metals with Group 1 in melting point, density, strength, hardness and reactivity.
Give examples of transition metal properties using Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni and Cu.
Describe variable ion charges, coloured compounds and catalyst use of transition elements.

units.title: 4.2 Bonding, structure, and the properties of matter

topics.title: 4.2.1 Chemical bonds, ionic, covalent and metallic

outcomes.text: Name the three strong bond types and the particles in each: ions, shared electron pairs, delocalised electrons.
Match ionic, covalent and metallic bonding to metal/non-metal compounds, non-metals and metals/alloys.
Explain bonding in terms of electrostatic forces and electron transfer or sharing.
Describe electron transfer from metal to non-metal atoms, giving ions with noble gas electronic structures.
Draw dot and cross diagrams for Group 1 and 2 metals with Group 6 and 7 non-metals.
Work out ion charges from the group number for Groups 1, 2, 6 and 7.
Describe an ionic compound as a giant lattice held by electrostatic attraction in all directions.
Deduce that a compound is ionic from a diagram of sodium chloride's structure.
Describe limitations of dot and cross, ball and stick and 2D/3D diagrams of ionic structures.
Work out an empirical formula from a model showing the ions.
Describe covalent bonds as shared electron pairs and recognise small molecules from their formulae.
Identify polymers and giant covalent structures such as diamond and silicon dioxide.
Draw dot and cross diagrams for H2, Cl2, O2, N2, HCl, water, ammonia and methane.
Represent bonds in molecules, polymer repeat units and giant structures using lines for single bonds.
Describe limitations of molecule diagrams and deduce a molecular formula from a model.
Describe a metal as a regular giant structure of atoms with delocalised outer electrons.
Explain that sharing delocalised electrons gives strong metallic bonds, and recognise metallic structures in diagrams.

topics.title: 4.2.2 How bonding and structure are related to the properties of substances

outcomes.text: Name solid, liquid and gas and the melting, freezing, boiling and condensing points.
Use the particle model to explain changes of state and why stronger forces mean higher melting and boiling points.
Predict states at different temperatures from data and recognise atoms lack bulk properties.
Explain limitations of the solid-sphere particle model (higher tier).
Write (s), (l), (g) and (aq) in equations for reactions in the specification.
Explain high melting and boiling points of ionic compounds from many strong lattice bonds.
Explain why ionic compounds conduct when molten or dissolved but not as solids.
Explain low melting and boiling points as weak intermolecular forces being overcome, not covalent bonds.
Explain that larger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces and that small molecules do not conduct.
Explain that polymers are solids because of strong covalent bonds and relatively strong intermolecular forces.
Explain very high melting points of giant covalent structures such as diamond, graphite and silica.
Recognise polymers and giant covalent structures from bonding diagrams.
Explain high melting points of metals from strong metallic bonding.
Explain that layers of atoms let pure metals bend, and why alloys are harder through distorted layers.
Explain electrical conduction in metals by moving delocalised electrons.
Explain thermal conduction in metals by energy transfer through delocalised electrons.

topics.title: 4.2.3 Structure and bonding of carbon

outcomes.text: Explain diamond's hardness, high melting point and non-conduction from four covalent bonds per carbon.
Describe graphite's hexagonal layers with three bonds per carbon and one delocalised electron.
Explain graphite's properties and compare it to metals through delocalised electrons.
Describe graphene as a single layer of graphite and explain its properties and uses.
Recognise fullerenes, Buckminsterfullerene and nanotubes from structure descriptions.
Give uses of fullerenes including carbon nanotubes.

topics.title: 4.2.4 Bulk and surface properties of matter including nanoparticles (chemistry only)

outcomes.text: Define nanoscience as 1-100 nm and compare nanoparticles with fine and coarse particles.
Explain that shrinking a cube by ten times raises surface area to volume ratio ten times.
Explain why nanoparticles differ from bulk materials and need smaller quantities.
Compare nano dimensions with atoms and molecules.
Name nanoparticle uses in medicine, electronics, cosmetics, sun creams, deodorants and catalysts.
Evaluate nanoparticle use for a purpose and explain possible risks.

topics.title: 4.3.1 Chemical measurements, conservation of mass and the quantitative interpretation of chemical equations

outcomes.text: State that no atoms are lost or made so reactant mass equals product mass.
Balance symbol equations and use multipliers before formulae and in subscripts.
Calculate relative formula mass as the sum of relative atomic masses.
Show that reactant and product formula masses balance in an equation.
Calculate percentage by mass of an element in a compound.
Explain apparent mass gain or loss when a gas is a reactant or product, such as oxide formation or carbonate decomposition.
Explain mass changes in open systems using the balanced equation and particle model.
Explain that every measurement has uncertainty and show the distribution of results.
Use the range about the mean as a measure of uncertainty.

topics.title: 4.3.2 Use of amount of substance in relation to masses of pure substances

outcomes.text: Define the mole and Avogadro constant (6.02 x 10^23) and say a mole's mass in grams equals relative formula mass (higher tier).
Convert between mass and moles using relative formula mass.
Interpret balanced equations in moles and calculate reactant and product masses from a given mass (higher tier).
Convert masses to moles and whole-number ratios to balance an equation (higher tier).
Explain that the limiting reactant is used up first and sets the product amount (higher tier).
Calculate mass of solute from concentration in g/dm3 and volume.
Relate solute mass and solution volume to concentration (higher tier).

topics.title: 4.3.3 Yield and atom economy of chemical reactions (chemistry only)

outcomes.text: Give reasons actual yield is below the calculated amount: reversible reactions, losses, side reactions.
Calculate percentage yield, and theoretical mass from a balanced equation (higher tier).
Define atom economy and explain why high values matter for sustainability and cost.
Calculate percentage atom economy from a balanced equation.
Choose a reaction pathway using atom economy, yield, rate, equilibrium and by-products (higher tier).

topics.title: 4.3.4 Using concentrations of solutions in mol/dm3 (chemistry only)

outcomes.text: Calculate moles or mass of solute from concentration in mol/dm3 and volume (higher tier).
Find an unknown concentration from the reacting volumes of two solutions (higher tier).

topics.title: 4.3.5 Use of amount of substance in relation to volumes of gases (chemistry only) (HT only)

outcomes.text: State that equal moles of gases occupy equal volumes and one mole is 24 dm3 at room temperature and pressure.
Calculate gas volumes from mass and relative formula mass, and from a balanced equation.

topics.title: 4.4.1 Reactivity of metals

outcomes.text: Describe metals reacting with oxygen to form oxides and define oxidation and reduction as gain or loss of oxygen.
Link reactivity to the tendency to form positive ions and place K, Na, Li, Ca, Mg, Zn, Fe, Cu in order.
Describe reactions of these metals with water and dilute acids at room temperature.
Explain displacement of a less reactive metal and deduce reactivity order from experimental results.
Explain why unreactive metals occur native while most are compounds needing extraction.
Describe extracting metals less reactive than carbon by reducing their oxides with carbon.
Identify what is oxidised or reduced as gain or loss of oxygen and evaluate extraction processes from information.

subtopics.title: Oxidation and reduction as electron transfer

outcomes.text: Define oxidation as electron loss and reduction as electron gain (higher tier).
Write ionic equations for displacement and identify oxidised and reduced species in half equations.

topics.title: 4.4.2 Reactions of acids

outcomes.text: State that acids react with magnesium, zinc and iron to give salts and hydrogen.
Explain these as redox reactions in terms of electrons (higher tier).
Describe acids neutralised by alkalis, bases and carbonates to give salts, water and carbon dioxide.
Name salts from the acid used and the positive ion, and predict products.
Use common ion formulae to deduce the formulae of salts.
Describe making a pure dry soluble salt from an acid and an excess insoluble solid, filtering and crystallising.
Say acids produce H+ ions and alkalis OH- ions, and neutralisation is H+ plus OH- making water.
Use the 0-14 pH scale and universal indicator or pH probe to identify acids and alkalis.
Describe a titration with strong acids and alkalis using an indicator to find reacting volumes (chemistry only).
Calculate quantities in titrations in mol/dm3 and g/dm3 (higher tier).
Distinguish strong (fully ionised) from weak (partly ionised) acids, and dilute from concentrated (higher tier).
Explain that each pH unit is a tenfold change in hydrogen ion concentration.

topics.title: 4.4.3 Electrolysis

outcomes.text: Explain electrolytes as molten or dissolved ionic compounds whose ions move to the electrodes.
Say cations go to the cathode and anions to the anode where they are discharged; write half equations (higher tier).
Predict products of electrolysing molten binary ionic compounds, such as lead bromide.
Explain when electrolysis is used to extract metals and why it needs large amounts of energy.
Describe aluminium extraction from aluminium oxide in cryolite with carbon anodes, and why the anode is replaced.
Explain which ions discharge in aqueous solutions using relative reactivity and water's H+ and OH- ions.
Predict products at the cathode and anode for solutions of a single ionic compound.
Say cathode reactions are reductions (ions gain electrons) and anode reactions are oxidations (ions lose electrons) (higher tier).
Write half equations such as 2H+ + 2e- to H2 and 4OH- to O2 + 2H2O + 4e-.

topics.title: 4.5.1 Exothermic and endothermic reactions

outcomes.text: Explain energy conservation in reactions and why exothermic products have less energy than reactants.
Classify reactions as exothermic or endothermic by the surroundings' temperature change and give examples.
Evaluate uses such as hand warmers, self-heating cans and sports injury packs.
Define activation energy as the minimum energy colliding particles need to react.
Draw reaction profiles for exothermic and endothermic reactions showing activation energy and overall energy change.
Use a reaction profile to identify a reaction as exothermic or endothermic.
Explain that bond breaking takes in energy and bond making releases it (higher tier).
Calculate overall energy change from bond energies and link its sign to exothermic or endothermic.

topics.title: 4.5.2 Chemical cells and fuel cells (chemistry only)

outcomes.text: Describe a simple cell made of two different metals in an electrolyte and what sets its voltage.
Explain batteries as cells in series and contrast non-rechargeable with rechargeable cells.
Interpret metal reactivity data and evaluate the use of cells.
Describe a hydrogen fuel cell oxidising hydrogen to water to produce a potential difference.
Evaluate hydrogen fuel cells against rechargeable batteries.
Write electrode half equations for the hydrogen fuel cell (higher tier).

units.title: 4.6 The rate and extent of chemical change

topics.title: 4.6.1 Rate of reaction

outcomes.text: Calculate mean rate from quantity of reactant used or product formed over time, in g/s or cm3/s.
Draw and interpret quantity-time graphs.
Use tangent slopes to find rate at a time, with gradient calculations and mol/s at higher tier.
Recall how concentration, pressure, surface area, temperature and catalysts change rate.
Explain reactions needing collisions with enough energy (activation energy).
Explain how concentration, pressure and surface area raise collision frequency.
Explain how temperature raises collision frequency and energy.
Explain particle size effects through surface area to volume ratio and simple proportionality.
State that catalysts speed reactions without being used up, and that enzymes are biological catalysts.
Explain catalysis as an alternative pathway with lower activation energy, shown on a reaction profile.
Identify catalysts from their effect and absence from the equation.

topics.title: 4.6.2 Reversible reactions and dynamic equilibrium

outcomes.text: Describe reversible reactions where products form reactants again, and how conditions change direction.
Explain that if one direction is exothermic the other is endothermic by the same amount of energy.
Explain equilibrium in a closed system as forward and reverse rates being equal.
Explain that equilibrium amounts depend on conditions and the system counteracts changes (higher tier).
Predict effects of concentration changes on the equilibrium position.
Predict effects of temperature changes for endothermic and exothermic reactions.
Predict pressure effects by comparing numbers of gas molecules on each side.

topics.title: 4.7.1 Carbon compounds as fuels and feedstock

outcomes.text: Describe crude oil as a finite resource formed from buried ancient plankton, a mixture mostly of hydrocarbons.
Give the alkane general formula CnH2n+2 and name methane, ethane, propane and butane.
Recognise alkanes from their formulae and displayed structures.
Explain fractional distillation of crude oil into fractions of similar carbon number using evaporation and condensation.
Name fuels and petrochemical products made from fractions.
State how boiling point, viscosity and flammability change with molecule size.
Describe complete combustion producing carbon dioxide and water, and write balanced equations for it.
Describe catalytic and steam cracking conditions and why cracking meets demand for small-molecule fuels.
Say cracking gives alkanes and alkenes, and that bromine water turns from orange to colourless with alkenes.
Balance cracking equations and explain how modern life depends on hydrocarbons.

topics.title: 4.7.2 Reactions of alkenes and alcohols (chemistry only)

outcomes.text: Describe alkenes as unsaturated hydrocarbons with a C=C bond and formula CnH2n.
Name ethene, propene, butene and pentene and recognise alkenes from formulae.
Explain that alkenes burn with smoky flames from incomplete combustion.
Describe addition of hydrogen, water and halogens across the C=C bond with conditions.
Draw displayed formulae of the first four alkenes and their addition products.
Name methanol, ethanol, propanol and butanol and recognise the -OH group.
Describe alcohols reacting with sodium, burning, dissolving in water and being oxidised, plus their uses.
Describe ethanol made by fermenting sugar with yeast and the conditions needed.
Name methanoic, ethanoic, propanoic and butanoic acid and recognise the -COOH group.
Describe reactions with carbonates, dissolving in water and reacting with alcohols to make esters.
Explain why carboxylic acids are weak acids using ionisation and pH (higher tier).

topics.title: 4.7.3 Synthetic and naturally occurring polymers (chemistry only)

outcomes.text: Describe monomers joining to form polymers such as poly(ethene) with a repeating unit with the monomer's atoms.
Recognise addition polymers and monomers by the C=C group and draw polymer formation from an alkene.
Explain condensation polymerisation using monomers with two functional groups that lose small molecules like water (higher tier).
Describe making a polyester from a diol and a dicarboxylic acid.
Explain amino acids having two functional groups and polymerising into polypeptides and proteins (higher tier).
Describe DNA as two nucleotide polymer chains in a double helix encoding genetic instructions.
Name monomers of proteins, starch and cellulose.

topics.title: 4.8.1 Purity, formulations and chromatography

outcomes.text: Define a pure substance chemically and use melting and boiling point data to tell pure from impure.
Define a formulation as a designed mixture with measured components and identify examples.
Explain paper chromatography with stationary and mobile phases separating mixtures.
Interpret chromatograms to judge purity and calculate Rf values.

topics.title: 4.8.2 Identification of common gases

outcomes.text: Test for hydrogen with a burning splint giving a pop.
Test for oxygen with a glowing splint that relights.
Test for carbon dioxide with limewater turning milky.
Test for chlorine with damp litmus paper that bleaches white.

topics.title: 4.8.3 Identification of ions by chemical and spectroscopic means (chemistry only)

outcomes.text: Identify lithium, sodium, potassium, calcium and copper ions from flame colours and note masking in mixtures.
Identify aluminium, calcium and magnesium ions by white precipitates with sodium hydroxide, and aluminium dissolving in excess.
Identify copper(II), iron(II), iron(III) by blue, green and brown precipitates, and write balanced equations.
Test for carbonates with dilute acid and limewater.
Test for halides with silver nitrate and nitric acid: white, cream and yellow precipitates.
Test for sulfates with barium chloride and hydrochloric acid giving a white precipitate.
State that instrumental methods are accurate, sensitive and rapid compared with chemical tests.
Describe flame emission spectroscopy and interpret line spectra to identify ions and concentrations.

topics.title: 4.9.1 The composition and evolution of the Earth's atmosphere

outcomes.text: Give the proportions of today's atmosphere: about 80% nitrogen, 20% oxygen and small amounts of other gases.
Describe the volcanic-outgassing theory of the early atmosphere and the formation of the oceans.
Explain how dissolving carbon dioxide and carbonate sediments reduced carbon dioxide.
Interpret evidence and evaluate theories about the early atmosphere.

subtopics.title: How oxygen and carbon dioxide changed

outcomes.text: Explain that algae and plants produced oxygen by photosynthesis from about 2.7 billion years ago.
Explain that photosynthesis, sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels lowered carbon dioxide.
Describe the main atmospheric changes and how limestone, coal, crude oil and natural gas formed.

topics.title: 4.9.2 Carbon dioxide and methane as greenhouse gases

outcomes.text: Name water vapour, carbon dioxide and methane as greenhouse gases that keep Earth warm enough for life.
Describe the greenhouse effect using short and long wavelength radiation interacting with matter.
Recall two human activities that increase carbon dioxide and two that increase methane.
Evaluate the quality of climate change evidence, its uncertainties and the role of peer review.
Describe four potential effects of climate change from rising average temperature.
Discuss the scale, risk and environmental implications of climate change.
Define carbon footprint as greenhouse gas emissions over a product's whole life cycle.
Describe actions to cut carbon dioxide and methane emissions and why they may be limited.

topics.title: 4.9.3 Common atmospheric pollutants and their sources

outcomes.text: Explain how burning fuels releases carbon monoxide, soot, sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides.
Predict combustion products from the fuel's composition and burning conditions.
Describe carbon monoxide as a toxic, colourless, odourless gas.
Explain that sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides cause respiratory problems and acid rain, and particulates cause global dimming.

topics.title: 4.10.1 Using the Earth's resources and obtaining potable water

outcomes.text: Give examples of natural products replaced or supplemented by agricultural and synthetic ones.
Distinguish finite from renewable resources and define sustainable development.
Interpret resource data from charts, graphs and tables using orders of magnitude.
Distinguish potable water from chemically pure water.
Describe producing potable water from fresh water by source choice, filter beds and sterilising with chlorine, ozone or UV.
Describe desalination by distillation or reverse osmosis and why it needs much energy.
Describe sewage treatment: screening, sedimentation, anaerobic digestion of sludge and aerobic treatment of effluent.
Compare how easily potable water is obtained from waste, ground and salt water.
Describe phytomining and bioleaching to get copper from low-grade ores (higher tier).
Evaluate these methods and describe obtaining copper by displacement with iron or electrolysis.

topics.title: 4.10.2 Life cycle assessment and recycling

outcomes.text: List the LCA stages: raw materials, manufacture and packaging, use, and disposal with transport.
Explain why LCA is not fully objective and how abbreviated LCAs can be misused.
Carry out a simple comparative LCA of plastic and paper shopping bags.
Explain how reduce, reuse and recycle lower resource use, energy, waste and environmental impact.
Describe recycling of glass and metals, including scrap steel added to blast-furnace iron.
Evaluate ways of reducing the use of limited resources from given information.

topics.title: 4.10.3 Using materials (chemistry only)

outcomes.text: Define corrosion and rusting, and show that iron needs both air and water to rust.
Describe barrier protection by greasing, painting and electroplating, and aluminium's oxide layer.
Explain sacrificial protection and galvanising using relative reactivity.
Recall compositions and uses of bronze, brass, gold alloys (carats), steels and aluminium alloys.
Compare high and low carbon steel and stainless steel, and evaluate unfamiliar alloy data.
Describe making soda-lime and borosilicate glass and clay ceramics.
Explain LD and HD poly(ethene) from ethene, and thermosoftening versus thermosetting polymers by structure.
Describe composites as matrix plus reinforcement and recall examples.
Compare material properties quantitatively and select materials for uses.

topics.title: 4.10.4 The Haber process and the use of NPK fertilisers (chemistry only)

outcomes.text: Describe making ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen over an iron catalyst at about 450 C and 200 atmospheres.
Recall sources of the nitrogen and hydrogen, and explain recycling of unreacted gases and liquefying ammonia.
Explain the trade-off between rate and equilibrium position, and how conditions reflect cost and supply (higher tier).
Explain that NPK fertilisers are formulations of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium compounds.
Describe making ammonium salts and nitric acid from ammonia, and treating phosphate rock with acids.
Compare industrial fertiliser production with laboratory preparation.

topics.title: 4.11 Key ideas

outcomes.text: Explain that matter is made of atoms of about 100 elements showing periodic patterns explained by atomic structure.
Explain bonding by electron transfer or sharing, and why molecule shape and giant structure affect behaviour.
Explain that reactions face barriers so rates differ, occur by proton transfer, electron transfer or electron sharing, and conserve energy.
